records.sourceFile: The effects of three hamstring programmes on strength and sprinting performance in female footballers - A randomised controlled trial.pdf

paper.citation: Whyte E, O'Connor S, Connolly A, Hession E, Kennedy J, O'Boyle B, et al. The effects of three hamstring programmes on strength and sprinting performance in female footballers: A randomised controlled trial. PLoS One. 2026;21(2):e0342529.
paper.abstract: Thirty-five female Gaelic footballers completed a supervised 4-week programme of Nordic hamstring exercise (NHE), single leg hamstring bridge (SLHB) or razor hamstring curl (RHC). Isometric knee flexor and hip extensor strength rose over time in all three groups, but group-by-time interactions were not significant and sprint performance did not change significantly.
paper.tldr: In 35 female Gaelic footballers, strength rose after four weeks of NHE, single leg bridge or razor curl, but the three exercises did not differ significantly and no sprint measure changed significantly. With no non-strengthening control group, the authors say the gains may reflect regular training, so this does not prove the exercises caused them or that one exercise is best.
paper.methods: Randomized controlled trial with allocation to NHE, SLHB or RHC by a 6-block pattern, two supervised sessions per week for 4 weeks, and no non-strengthening control group. Outcomes were isometric knee flexor and hip extensor torque, peak eccentric knee flexor torque during NHE, and 0-5, 0-10 and 0-30 m sprint times with FH0, V0 and Pmax, analysed by two-way mixed ANOVA (Wilcoxon and Kruskal-Wallis for NHE eccentric torque).
paper.findings: Isometric knee flexor torque rose about 11% to 17% in each group, and isometric hip extensor torque rose at 0 and 30 degrees hip flexion, with large main effects of time pooled across groups. Eccentric NHE torque rose 11.6% to 18.0% in the NHE and razor curl groups but only 0.1% to 1.9% in the bridge group, with no significant group effect. No group-by-time interaction was significant for the isometric measures, a dominant hip extensor group effect did not survive Bonferroni-adjusted post hoc comparison, and 0-5, 0-10 and 0-30 m sprint times, FH0, V0 and Pmax showed no significant time, group or interaction effects.
paper.limitations: There was no control group without strengthening work, so gains cannot be separated from regular training, and participants and assessors were not blinded. The abstract says 35 were randomized, while the Discussion says 47 were randomized and 35 completed; the abstract lists 0-15 m sprint times while the results and Table 4 report 10 m. The 35 completers were below the study's own power target of 36.
paper.practicalImplications: Any of the three exercises may be used for a 4-week strength block in female footballers; the authors suggest NHE may be more practically impactful for hip extensor strength, though no exercise differed significantly. Do not expect a sprint time gain from a block of this length, since the authors suggest longer interventions if sprint performance is the target.
paper.athleteDev: Knee flexor and hip extensor strength rose over a 4-week block of any of the three exercises, but without a control group the gain cannot be credited to the exercises, and the single leg bridge did not raise eccentric NHE torque. No sprint time or mechanical measure changed significantly, so this paper gives no evidence that a block of this length will improve sprint speed.
paper.rtp: It cannot inform return to sport. Players were healthy (no hamstring injury in the previous 6 months), and the study measured strength and sprint change with no injured group and no rehabilitation or re-injury outcome, so it gives no clearance or readiness criteria.

records.sourceFile: Effects of resisted sprint training on sprint, jump, and change-of-direction performance in athletes - a systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Li C, Chen L, Zhang Q. Effects of resisted sprint training on sprint, jump, and change-of-direction performance in athletes: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Front Physiol. 2025;16:1711992.
paper.abstract: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 16 studies (404 participants) comparing resisted sprint training with unresisted sprinting or regular training on linear sprint, vertical jump and change-of-direction performance in athletes. Both resisted and unresisted sprinting improved sprint and change of direction, and resisted sprinting beat unresisted sprinting only for change of direction (p = 0.043).
paper.tldr: Resisted and unresisted sprinting both improved linear sprint and change-of-direction performance, and resisted sprinting was not clearly better for overall sprint speed (p = 0.057). Its edge was a borderline change-of-direction advantage and, by the authors' subgroup analysis, the 0-10 m sprint.
paper.methods: PRISMA review registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251103833), searching seven databases (PubMed, Web of Science, MEDLINE, CENTRAL, SPORTDiscus, Scopus and Embase) from inception to 12 July 2025. Randomized and non-randomized controlled trials compared RST with UST or regular training in competitive or recreational athletes over 4-12 weeks; risk of bias was rated with RoB 2, certainty with GRADE, and analysis used random-effects models in Stata/MP 18.0.
paper.findings: Within-group, RST improved linear sprint (SMD 0.65) and COD (SMD 1.10), and its vertical jump effect was reported as significant (SMD -0.38, p = 0.013) though printed with a negative sign. UST improved linear sprint (SMD 0.42) and COD (SMD 0.60) but not vertical jump (SMD -0.03, p = 0.872). RST beat UST for COD (p = 0.043) but not for overall sprint (p = 0.057) or jump (p = 0.102); the authors report larger RST benefits at 0-10 m (SMD 0.81 vs 0.34 at 0-20 m and 0.71 at 0-30 m) and in youth (SMD 0.81 vs 0.72 in adults), and say RST beat regular training for sprint and jump (p < 0.001) but not COD (p = 0.064).
paper.limitations: Sport, sex, training level, sled load, sprint distance and volume varied, most studies involved male soccer players, and the authors say the small number of COD and jump studies reduces confidence in those estimates. Egger's test suggested publication bias for sprint (RST vs UST, p = 0.003), and the trim-and-fill estimate (SMD 0.55, 95% CI -0.12 to 1.22) crosses zero although the authors call it robust. The tables do not match the text: Table 6 gives the regular-training sprint row as SMD 0.18 (95% CI 0.00 to 0.36) while the discussion reports SMD 0.53 for RST against regular training and Table 8 gives the regular-training COD row as SMD -0.53 (p = 0.686) with a CI that excludes its own point estimate, and the jump SMD sign is never explained.
paper.practicalImplications: Resisted sprinting is a reasonable option when short acceleration and change of direction are the goals, but this review does not show it beats plain sprinting for overall sprint speed. The authors' suggestion to pair it with vertical strength or plyometric work for jump power is their recommendation, not something the included trials tested.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff can use resisted sprinting as one sprint and change-of-direction option, with the authors' subgroup results pointing to the 0-10 m phase and youth athletes. Unresisted sprinting produced similar overall sprint gains, so it remains a valid main method.
paper.rtp: Not designed for return to sport: the studies were in trained athletes and the review does not assess injury outcomes, so it cannot guide reintroduction of sprint loading after injury. The authors name injury prevention and risk as a research need.

records.sourceFile: The Relationship Between Inter-limb Asymmetry and Sprinting Performance in Sprint Athletes - A Systematic Review.pdf

paper.citation: D'Hondt J, Chapelle L, Van Handenhoven J, Stalmans J, Aerenhouts D. The Relationship Between Inter-limb Asymmetry and Sprinting Performance in Sprint Athletes: A Systematic Review. Sports Med Open. 2026;12:146.
paper.abstract: Systematic review of 10 studies (from 4,811 screened records) on the association between lower-limb inter-limb asymmetry and sprinting performance in healthy, injury-free sprint athletes. Associations were limited overall, with task- and metric-specific links in individual studies, and the authors call the evidence mixed.
paper.tldr: In sprinters, most measures of left-right asymmetry were not linked to sprint performance, and the few links came from single small studies rated very low certainty. Asymmetry on its own is not a strong reason to change a sprinter's training.
paper.methods: PRISMA 2020 review (PROSPERO CRD420251140520) searching PubMed, Scopus, SPORTDiscus and Web of Science to 17 March 2026, plus citation tracking, for studies of lower-limb asymmetry and sprint performance (up to 400 m) in healthy, injury-free sprint athletes of any age and level. Quality was rated with a modified 10-item Downs and Black checklist (scores 6-8/10) and certainty with GRADE; results were synthesized narratively.
paper.findings: Most asymmetry measures showed no significant association, including all kinetic measures in 64 highly trained sprinters (Nagahara et al.) and short-term changes in asymmetry over one month in 13 sprinters (Gleadhill et al.). Single small studies reported sex-specific kinematic links in 16 world-class sprinters (r = -0.86 in males, r = 0.81 in females), net ankle work asymmetry linked to 60 m velocity in 8 males (r = 0.90), and textile EMG asymmetry correlated with 50 m time in 8 elite females (rs 0.36 to 0.59, significance not stated). In Jamaican cohorts, knee joint width and composite asymmetry had significant but very small associations with 90 m and 180 m velocity and IAAF scores (R2 0.02 to 0.05).
paper.limitations: Asymmetry dimensions, equations, tasks, sex, age and training status varied widely, so the authors judged a meta-analysis inappropriate, and all outcomes were downgraded for risk of bias and imprecision to very low certainty. The text conflicts on the Trivers results: the results report knee joint width asymmetry as positively associated with 90 m velocity (beta 0.21 to 0.24), while the discussion says it was linked to lower velocities; the results also once refer to a 'systematic review with meta-analysis' although none was done.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors conclude that reducing asymmetry does not need to be a central focus of sprint training for performance, given the inconsistent links. If asymmetry is measured, use the same task and metric over time and know the test's reliability, since most included studies did not.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff should not assume that reducing a between-limb difference will improve sprint speed, because no included study tested that. Interpret any asymmetry score against the specific test and metric used, because the few associations were task-, metric- and sex-specific.
paper.rtp: Limited application to return to sport: the review included only healthy, injury-free athletes, so it cannot show whether asymmetry after injury affects sprint readiness or re-injury risk.
